To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the phenology of trees (particularly dominant species such as quaking aspens, white oaks, and American beehs) can be estimated using MODIS data and (2) the phenology observed by citizen scientists is correlated with MODIS phenology.

the phenology of trees can be accurately measured using citizen science and that the results are highly correlated with remote sensing measurements of land surface phenology, particularly in forested areas.

(1) the phenological observations made by citizen scientists are highly correlated with land surface phenology, (2) this relationship is strongest when the analysis is restricted to forested land, and (3) quality control of the citizen scientists’ phenological observations improves the relationship between ground-based and remotely-sensed phenology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synergistic use of citizen science and remote sensing to measure plant phenology at continental scales.
the synergistic use of citizen science and remote sensing for continental-scale measurements of forest tree phenology.
the use of remote sensing and ground based phenological observations for the study of climate change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of citizen science and remote sensing for continental scale measurements of forest phenology can be synergistic, but the data must be appropriately quality controlled and the analysis must be restricted to forested pixels.

there is a high degree of agreement between ground- and remotely-sensed phenology for dominant forest tree species, and that the agreement is highest when the remotely-sensed data is aggregated over forested areas.
the correlation between ground and remote observations was high for forested pixels, and the quality of the correlation could be improved by restricting the data to the forested pixels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that it is possible to use MODIS data to make accurate predictions of the phenology of trees that dominate the forest canopy.
there is a high correlation between the phenological observations of individual trees (dominant forest trees) and the phenological observations for the surrounding forested area.

citizen scientists’ phenological observations are highly correlated with MODIS phenology in forested pixels and that this correlation is highest when observations are restricted to dominant trees in the surrounding canopy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of remote sensing phenology to predict ground-based phenology is feasible for dominant forest trees.
citizen scientists’ observations can be used to validate and improve the accuracy of remote observations of phenology and to help understand the causes of spatial and temporal variation.
the phenology of dominant forest trees can be reliably estimated by remote sensing and that the phenology derived from these observations correlates well with ground-based observations.
